thread.title: Long: Celebrating Charles Schulz, the creator of the 'longest story'
thread.title_full: Long: Celebrating Charles Schulz, the creator of the 'longest story'

author: John Long
title: Long: Celebrating Charles Schulz, the creator of the 'longest story'
text:
Suppose I asked you to draw a series of pictures that together tell a cohesive, amusing story. (I can’t draw even a passable stick figure, but maybe you could pull it off.) Could you do it again, with originality? Once more?
How about 17,897 times?
That is exactly what the masterful Charles M. Schulz pulled off over half a century, starting with the first strip 75 years ago this month. In so doing he enriched modern culture (and my own life) so thoroughly that it’s worth a bit of retrospection.
I’ve written before about how much a “Peanuts” fan I’ve always been. It was in the daily paper each afternoon when I got home from school, and later greeted me over breakfast before work.
The TV specials were much-anticipated, practically memorized hallmarks of passing seasons. The gang appeared on Broadway, floated above big-city parades, and even went to the moon.
It all started with a shy, withdrawn kid who liked to draw. “Sparky” Schulz grew up in Minnesota and served in the army during World War II; he never wavered from his ambition to be an artist.
He had published some one-panel cartoons here and there (even featuring characters named Charlie Brown), but in 1950 Sparky jumped at a chance to work with United Features Syndicate.
He pitched a one-panel cartoon titled “Li’l Folks” but it quickly evolved into a comic strip of three or four panels. The syndicator changed the name to “Peanuts,” something of a non sequitur which Schulz never liked; but frankly I can’t imagine 50 years of the other name.
From such slow beginnings a multi-billion dollar empire was born. Greeting cards, sweatshirts, food products, toys, and a million other products sported the iconic characters. I remember fondly a floating Snoopy soap dish I had.
As a kid I frequently checked out the anthology books from the library, so I imagine I read nearly all of those 17,897 strips multiple times. I never gave a lot of thought to why I like “Peanuts” so much in my childhood. Only as an adult perusing histories and analyses of the strip did it dawn on me.
The kids weren’t realistic kids. They were precocious and hilarious. They had only passing interest in the usual childhood activities. They talked like adults — and particularly smart, observant, well-informed adults.
Children being child-like wasn’t as funny to me (for instance, I never got nearly as much delight from “The Family Circus” in the funnies). Where else could you find a kid named 5, because his parents were protesting the impersonal nature of modern society?
A kid who played Beethoven on his toy piano?
Linus was self-aware of his neuroses enough to invent the term security blanket; his crabby sister Lucy dispensed psychiatric advice from a homemade stand for a nickel a pop.
In fact, pretty much everything I knew as a kid about Beethoven, psychiatry, Word War I aviation, ophthalmology, cats next door, and a host of other topics I gleaned from “Peanuts.”
Adults, incidentally, never appeared “on screen” in the comic strip, though some TV versions broke such canon on occasion.
“Peanuts” has been called the “longest story” ever told by a single human being. Schulz drew every one of those strips himself; he never used unnamed collaborators to ink his work like other cartoonists do. He wrote every single word himself, and he was a darned good writer.
Along the way he cogently explored the shared human experiences of disappointment and loss (“Winning isn’t funny,” Schulz once pointed out).
Charlie Brown never kicked that football or won a baseball game (except once by forfeit).
Love was intense (especially for 4- to 8-year-olds) and always unrequited: Sally for Linus, Lucy for Schroeder, Charlie Brown for the elusive Little Red-Haired Girl. The Great Pumpkin never came, but Linus’ faith somehow never wavered.
Everyone could relate to these characters, especially Charlie Brown, the ever-lovable, ever-sincere loser. Because in one way or another, at one time or another, we’re all Charlie Brown.
In late 1999, dying of cancer and a victim of diminished eyesight, Schulz announced his retirement. Unlike other cartoonists who bequeath their characters to other artists, the Schulz family made it clear that no one else will ever draw another original “Peanuts” strip (old strips continue in syndication).
The irreplaceable, irreplicable Sparky died on Feb. 12, 2000. Poetically, his final strip ran in the papers the next day. “How can I ever forget them?” the artist asked of his beloved characters. Indeed, how can any of us?
